name: Garveyism
scope: The doctrine of Marcus Garvey and the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in the 1910s-1920s: race-first Black nationalism and Pan-Africanism, Black economic self-reliance and a redeemed Africa for the Africans of the world, together with the UNIA's own civil religion (its ritual, Catechism and Chaplain-General) that Burkett's scholarship treats as part of Garveyism. Defining texts: Garvey's Philosophy and Opinions (ed. Amy Jacques Garvey) and the 1920 Declaration of Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World. Excluded: later movements that drew on Garvey (Rastafari, the Nation of Islam, Nkrumah-era Pan-Africanism) and the UNIA's later splinters.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: "I have no faith in the disarmament plan of the nations ... Any attempt at disarming when half of the world oppresses the other half is but a farce" (vol. II, speech on the disarmament conference).

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: "when races and nations provoke the ire of other races and nations by attempting to infringe upon their rights, war becomes inevitable, and the attempt in any way to free one's self or protect one's rights or heritage becomes justifiable" (art. 16).

arms-reduction.rationale: He calls the disarmament conference "all a joke" and says man will not disarm "until there is universal justice"; he urges Negroes to "get armed with organization" (vol. II).

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Declaration protests that Europeans "have parcelled out among them" Africa and that natives "are compelled to surrender their lands to aliens and are treated in most instances like slaves" (complaint III; art. 15).

consent-of-governed.rationale: "The government must be, therefore, an expression of the will of the people" (vol. I); the Declaration calls taxation without representation "unjust and tyrannous" (art. 8).

diaspora-return-right.rationale: The delegates "claim them as free citizens of Africa, the Motherland of all Negroes" (art. 1) and demand "Africa for the Africans at home and abroad" (art. 13); all Negroes have the right to travel the world (art. 36).

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: "we believe in the racial purity of both the Negro and white races"; the UNIA opposes the NAACP "on the miscegenation question" and calls social equality a "dangerous doctrine" that "would destroy the racial purity of both".

equal-moral-worth.rationale: "all men are created equal and entitled to the rights of life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness" (art. 1); "the Negro is entitled to even-handed justice before all courts of law and equity in whatever country he may be found" (art. 5).

ethnic-nation.rationale: "Africa for the Africans" on the principle of "Europe for the Europeans and Asia for the Asiatics" (Declaration, art. 13); vol. I: "every race must find a home".

historical-land-claim.rationale: "We believe in the inherent right of the Negro to possess himself of Africa, and that his possession of same shall not be regarded as an infringement on any claim or purchase made by any race or nation." (art. 14)

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: The programme is to gather the race into a redeemed Africa (arts. 1, 13, 14) rather than to make the homeland a cultural centre for a dispersed people.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Africa is "the Motherland of all Negroes" (art. 1) and "the vast continent of our forefathers" (art. 15); the UNIA anthem opens "Ethiopia, thou land of our fathers".

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: "the race can only be saved through a solid industrial foundation; and ... through political independence. Take away industry from a race; take away political freedom from a race, and you have a group of slaves." (vol. I)

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Vol. I lists "the great cry of Palestine for the Jews" with Ireland for the Irish and India for the Indians as the "political re-adjustment" whereby "every race must find a home".

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The Declaration claims Negroes everywhere as citizens of one Africa and demands Africa for Negroes "at home and abroad" (arts. 1, 13); Garvey was elected Provisional President of Africa.

morality-needs-religion.rationale: "It is only the belief and the confidence we have in a God why man is able to understand his own social institutions ... Take away the highest ideal: faith and confidence in a God, and mankind at large is reduced to savagery." (vol. I)

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: "Negroes, wheresoever they form a community among themselves, should be given the right to elect their own representatives" to legislatures and courts (art. 4), with "complete control of our social institutions" (art. 38).

national-resource-control.rationale: The Declaration condemns nations that "have seized the territories and inexhaustible natural wealth of Africa" and resolves "to reclaim the treasures and possession of the vast continent" (art. 15).

national-self-determination.rationale: "We believe in the self-determination of all peoples." (art. 27); vol. I: "every race must find a home".

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: "We declare it unjust for any country, State or nation to enact laws tending to hinder and obstruct the free immigration of Negroes on account of their race and color." (art. 34)

race-social-construct.rationale: Garvey treats the races as real and distinct: "we believe in the racial purity of both the Negro and white races" (Philosophy and Opinions, vol. II), and the Declaration speaks of "the supreme authority of our race in all things racial" (art. 2).

racial-community-economic-control.rationale: The race must "of our own initiative ... strike out to build industries, governments, and ultimately empires" (vol. I); the Declaration demands control of the race's own institutions (art. 38).

racial-group-interests.rationale: "we believe in the supreme authority of our race in all things racial" (art. 2); "We demand complete control of our social institutions without interference by any alien race" (art. 38).

racial-pride.rationale: The Declaration says the race "should in no way tolerate any insults that may be interpreted to mean disrespect to our color" (art. 10) and calls teaching that an alien race is superior "an insult to the Negro people of the world" (art. 31); vol. II praises "race pride".

racial-segregation-law.rationale: "We protest against segregated districts, separate public conveyances, industrial discrimination, lynchings and limitations of political privileges of any Negro citizen" (art. 20); the Declaration also protests Jim Crow cars (complaint V).

regional-resource-ownership.rationale: Art. 15 treats the natural wealth of Africa as the continent's own, to be reclaimed by its peoples.

state-harmful.rationale: Garvey wants a state: "Independence of nationality, independence of government, is the means of protecting" a people, and the race must "build industries, governments, and ultimately empires" (vol. I).

unions-good.rationale: Garvey warns the Negro worker "to be careful of the traps and pitfalls of white trade unionism" and advises him to organise by himself (vol. II); this is a warning about white unions, not a rejection of unions as such.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: "any law especially directed against the Negro to his detriment ... is unfair and immoral, and should not be respected" (art. 9); no native should respect a law that deprives him of his land (art. 7).

summary: Garveyism is the race-first Black nationalism and Pan-Africanism of Marcus Garvey and the Universal Negro Improvement Association. Its Declaration of Rights (1920) claims all Negroes as citizens of Africa and demands "Africa for the Africans at home and abroad", self-determination for all peoples, control of Africa's wealth and an end to segregation and lynching. Garvey held that races should keep their racial purity and that a race needs its own industry and government, and he founded politics on belief in God.
notes: Themes searched in the Philosophy and Opinions (vols. I-II), the Declaration of Rights and Burkett (1978): race and miscegenation, Africa and return, self-determination, colonialism, law and consent, segregation and immigration, religion, labour and communism, the Klan, disarmament and Zionism. The earlier pass's guessed zeros and "inferred" answers were nulled or kept only where Garvey or the Declaration states the position. Garvey's 1922 meeting with the Klan and his praise of its honesty (vol. II) are documented but state no position on any statement here. Most modern policy statements are null.
